en: Oṃ.
(Then Sampāti enters. Sampāti: Surely today my dear son Jaṭāyu approaches the nest in the Malaya cave to pay his respects; for so it is:

The movements of the great wings of the son of Śyeni proclaim his arrival—movements that cause the quarters to vanish and reappear in an instant, that turn clouds into mist and release flashing, distinct lightning, and that scatter rows of massive boulders nearby, reducing them to a jangling clatter. //1//

The netherworld is being inflated by the forceful wind rushing through the openings of the ocean—whose waters are shattered by surging waves and whose submarine fire is tossed far away—as it roars like a sudden rain-cloud at the night of universal destruction, fierce with the terrifying sound issuing loudly from the cavernous throat of the Boar-incarnate Vaikuṇṭha. //2//
(Entering, Jaṭāyu:
I descend from the sky onto a ridge of the Malaya mountain, whose slopes are encircled by the Kāverī river;
there dwells my noble brother, the bird Kāśyapa, like another lord of mountains whose wings have been torn away. (3)
As she took hold of my wings and began to weaken them, the pain of the effort of flying arose within me as well;
for the power of Time, known as old age, is the cause that obstructs all other powers, however pervasive they may be.
So this is the noble Sampāti, the king of vultures, who lived for many Manvantaras. Oh, what brotherly affection!
In a former age, because he was so excessively attached to me due to the playful habit of long-distance flight, his limbs were scorched by the sun;
yet, holding me up with his wings as I was a mere child, he protected me without fail out of compassion, shielding me from the burning heat. (5)
(Approaching) Noble Kāśyapa, Jaṭāyu greets you.
Sampāti: Come, come, my child! By you, a virtuous sovereign of the vultures, Śyenī has become a mother of sons, just as our grandmother Vinatā was by the heroic Garuḍa. (6)
(Embracing him) Dear Jaṭāyu, has the grief for the death of our father grown less for the noble Rāma due to the passage of time?
Jaṭāyu: His association with those advanced in knowledge and asceticism, his own steadfastness, and his rightful authority over protection dispel my dejection. (7)
Sampāti: Indeed, I have been informed by vultures, who were satiated with the flesh of Virādha, that Rāma has gone from Citrakūṭa to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga. (8)
And then, after Śarabhaṅga had offered his body into the sacrificial fire,
Rāma approached the sages, including Sutīkṣṇa and others.
Jaṭāyu: Certainly. Now, at the word of Agastya, Rāma resides in Pañcavaṭī.
Sampāti:

(Recalling after a long time) Ah! There is a place on the banks of the Godāvarī in Janasthāna called Pañcavaṭī. Dear Jaṭāyu, the vastness of the region and the great lapse of time rob me of my memory.
At the beginning of the Kalpa, my acquaintance with that place lasted as long as Viṣṇu’s foot, with the beautiful Gaṅgā as its banner, rose above him.
Even at the furthest limits, the circle of his power extends as far as the Lokāloka mountain, which marks the boundary of the seventh ocean.
Jaṭāyu: Once upon a time, Śūrpaṇakhā, desiring the bull of the Raghus, arrived there.
Sampāti: Oh, what lawlessness!
She who has lived through many ages—of whom the Tretā age is now the thirteenth—is not ashamed that she puts to shame even that child whose throat is still full of milk. (11)
And Jaṭāyu caused Lakṣmaṇa to cut off her ears, nose, and lips, as if to record a panegyric for his humiliation of the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa). //12//
Sampāti: In that case, has some persistent legal dispute been instigated against him by others?
Jaṭāyu: Indeed! By Rāmabhadra alone, fourteen thousand and fourteen rākṣasas, as well as the three—Dūṣaṇa, Khara, and Triśiras—were slain in battle. (13)

Sampāti: How wonderful! Or rather, it is no wonder that this great gateway of enmity has been flung open again toward the son of Daśaratha; thinking thus, I am utterly bewildered. Therefore, my dear Jaṭāyu, at this juncture, Sītā, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa must not be left by you for even a moment.
How indeed can the Ten-faced one endure the humiliation of his own uterine sister, as well as the repeated slaughter of his kinsmen?

Alas, the enemy who dwells nearby—a master blinded by pride, a master of illusion, and possessed of immeasurable prowess—makes the young ones difficult to protect; they must indeed be guarded with great skill. (14)
I too, having performed my daily rites at the ocean, shall meditate upon the transformation into supreme auspiciousness.
(Thus he exits. Jaṭāyu:
(Flying up and gesturing the act of traveling through the sky:)

Here I am, having arrived from the Malaya mountain with great speed, contracting the vastness of the sky as if drinking it up with a force as fierce as the wind of universal dissolution, and passing over the dense clusters of trees clinging to its slopes.

This is the mountain named Prasravaṇa, situated in the central region of Janasthāna; its caves are made resonant by the Godāvarī river, which is embraced by a forest whose surrounding areas are lush, pure, and densely covered with thickets of trees, and its dark blue hue is intensified by clouds that are constantly pouring down rain. And this is Pañcavaṭī.
(Reflecting) Ah! Rāma has been led far away in that direction by the painted deer, and Lakṣmaṇa follows him.
Therefore, having entered his hermitage, here is the Ten-necked One (Rāvaṇa) in his disguised form.
"Disaster! Disaster!
This wicked man, having placed the young bride upon a chariot yoked with thousands of donkeys that have the faces of piśācas, is going away somewhere. (17)
O descendant of Pulastya!

How could such a wicked thought arise in you—a man born of a lineage of lords of knowledge who were the upholders of the Lord’s Veda during the cosmic dissolutions; one who has bathed in the vows of the Veda;

a conqueror even of the abode of Indra; and one who, though a king, is proud of his asceticism? For such a person, neither reproachable conduct nor a low birth has ever occurred, so how has this evil intent been born? (18)
How can you not listen out of such contempt? Ah, you evil-souled, lowest of demons! Stop, stop!

May the son of Śyenī be satisfied by your limbs—whose neck-vessels are severed by his claws fierce as extremely sharp saws and whose bones crackle—as he drags the skull-peak from which your head was once thrust forward, while your lungs, spleen, liver, heart, warm blood, sinews, and network of entrails quiver and burst apart!
(Thus he exits. //The Interlude//
(Lakṣmaṇa enters. Alas, noble lady! Where are you? Alas, my noble brother suffers the bitter fruit of his fate because of Mārīca!
He bears a body agitated by mental anguish, shame, and distress—like wrath incarnate, like the fire of sorrow walking on foot. (20)

For instance: With the fierce fire of his wrath—vast, ill-contained, and paralyzed by a fortitude flashing within, as indicated by the formation of peaks upon his arched brow—bearing the likeness of a cloud whose interior contains a thunderbolt revealed by lightning, he resembles the ocean-treasury when the Vāḍava fire blazes in its midst and a column of smoke rises from its waters. (21)
(Then Rāma enters. Rāma:
This humiliation throbs intensely in my heart like a thunderbolt; my mind sinks as if into a terrible, blinding darkness, closed up by shame.
The grief born from my father’s calamity burns me; there is no remedy for it whatsoever, yet compassion toward the wretched Sītā pierces me again as if striking my very vitals. (22)
Lakṣmaṇa: Noble brother, noble brother! Truly, those such as you, whose deeds transcend the world, do not lose their composure even in the midst of hardships.

Rāma: Child, the deeds of Rāma are indeed superhuman. By them, those former kings who were the banners of the solar dynasty—those great oppressors by whose protection the worlds remained secure from all fear—were surpassed.

He who remained firm even at the end of aeons, the noble Jaṭāyu, was sent to heaven; and as for what was done to my wife in the forest, that which had been left undone by the world has now been accomplished by me. (23)
Alas, dear father Kāśyapa, king of birds! Where else could there be the birth of such a great, holy, and virtuous being as you, who have become a true ford for others?
Lakṣmaṇa: O long-lived one, I seem to see that final state of our father;
for that Sītā, whom you search for like a medicinal herb in forest after forest, and who is as dear to me as my own life—both of them have been carried off by Rāvaṇa.
Having spoken this very thing, my father ascended to the world of heroes.
Rāma: Dear child, these introductory remarks truly pierce the very vitals of my heart.
Lakṣmaṇa: Indeed so.
Rāma: What indeed could be done that would be equal to such an excess of humiliation?

Long ago my mind was set upon the slaughter of the Rākṣasa, for they are to be slain by many means. Even if only this much were accomplished here, how could there be peace for me? For there is no purpose other than the destruction of the entire race. (25)

Nevertheless, my child, my anger—massed together by its fierce intensity, steady in its course, as if drinking inwardly again and again, suddenly flaring up intensely, as if issuing forth in flames because no other object to be consumed is found—burns me like the Vāḍava fire in the ocean; therefore, save me! 26.

Lakṇa: These forests toward the southern direction, where various herds of wild animals are utterly terrified and the formidable mountain caves are overrun by packs of maddened and fierce beasts of prey, lie along these very paths; let us travel by them.
Rāma: Indeed, these regions of Janasthāna have never been seen by me before.

Lakṣmaṇa: Surely a considerable time has passed since we two departed from the Pañcavaṭī hermitage after cremating our father Āruṇi, the king of vultures, and consigning him to the fire; for the borders of Janasthāna are now far behind us. And since these forests ahead inspire such terror, this must surely be that western division of the Daṇḍaka forest known as Kuñjavat, inhabited by the headless demon Danu.
Rāma: That wicked-souled frog of the forest must certainly be seen.
(Offstage: Ho there! Who is present here? Let someone rescue a woman being dragged through the forest by this headless demon (*rakṣasa-kabandha*)!
For I am a female ascetic of the Śabara tribe named Śramaṇā, a perfected one (*siddhā*); I dwell in the hermitage of Mataṅga and have come here searching for Rāma. (27)
Rāma: Child Lakṣmaṇa, go.
Lakṣmaṇa: Here, I have gone.
(Thus he exits.
Rāma: My beloved, alas, alas! Where are you? Speak sweet words to me; for those who have been defeated, even such a diversion as lamenting is difficult to obtain.
Let the blameless descendant of Pulastya go; let the censure fall upon me instead, since now that enmity has taken root, he has repaid me many times over.
(Then Lakṣmaṇa and a female ascetic enter.

Lakṣmaṇa: O Noble Lady, that face—with its clusters of whiskers drenched in the blood flowing from the multitudes of creatures mangled by his cruel teeth like saws—and that body of hideous form belonging to the long-armed one, were not seen by the noble brother out of his curiosity regarding the Rākṣasa. (29)
"Noble Śramaṇa! This is the Noble One."
"O ascetic! May Your Majesty be victorious!"
Rāma: Now, what is the purpose of searching for us?
O ascetic, do you hear Vibhīṣaṇa, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa?
Rāma: Who does not hear of him?

O ascetic! As soon as Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and the others were slain by Your Majesty, he departed from his kinsmen for some reason and has been residing on Mount Ṛṣyamūka due to his friendship with Sugrīva. This letter is entrusted to him by himself.
(Thus he hands over the letter. Lakṣmaṇa: (Taking it, he reads: "Hail! Vibhīṣaṇa, having bowed to the divine Rāma, makes this representation."
For us whose fortunes have failed, there are only two supreme courses of action:
either that our dharma be upheld by you, or that you yourself become the protector of dharma. (30)
Rāma: Child, tell me, what message should be sent to our dear friend, the lord of Laṅkā, the venerable Great King Vibhīṣaṇa, who speaks thus?
Lakṣmaṇa: Since the Lord has stated that the Lord of Laṅkā is his dear friend, what remains for the message?
Rāma: It is exactly as Saumitri has said.
O Śramaṇā, we have been favored.
Lakṣmaṇa: Noble Śramaṇā, tell me: has there been any news of my noble sister due to her contact with Vibhīṣaṇa?

O ascetics, it does not exist in the present. However, when I was being carried away by that evil-souled wretch Rāvaṇa, my upper garment, from which the name of Manasūyā had slipped, fell; and that was seized by them.
Rāma: Alas, my beloved, dear companion in our dwelling in the great forest, daughter of the King of Videha!
(Thus he mimes concealing it.
Lakṣmaṇa: Noble lady, by whom was it taken, or for what reason?
O ascetic! Because of their partiality for the virtues of Rāma, [the monkeys] such as Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, Hanumān, and others were rendered mute in their efforts.

Rāma: Indeed, those great-souled ones, whose majesty is honored by the world and who act kindly without motive, must be seen. And that token of recognition, Sītā’s dwelling, has been heard of. Therefore, let us go toward Ṛṣyamūka for now.
"O Śramaṇā! Then let Your Majesty come this way, this way."

(They walk about. Lakṣmaṇa: "Hanūmān! Hanūmān!"—this is a great cry of praise for a hero. Regarding this venerable one, even while he was but newly born, wondrous and extraordinary feats are heard of which caused both gods and asuras to tremble. Moreover, it is said:
whatever prowess there is in drawing a thunderbolt, or whatever in the wind when it is fully risen...
And that which was in the mighty-armed Vālin, it was also in the heroic Hanumān.

O ascetic, such is the son born of the soil of the venerable Kesari, the preeminent monkey, the leader of a great troop residing on Mount Hemakūṭa—he who is named Hanumān, the son of Añjanā, whose progenitor is the blessed Wind-god. What need is there for Hanumān alone?

For those [monkeys] who drink up the waters of the ocean with their hollowed palms like coconut juice, and for whom a single tree—mostly Lakucas and Udumbaras—is sufficient to serve as the cause for uprooting mountain peaks.

Even countless millions of those monkeys—who are capable of violently tearing apart the entire Brahma-stambha as if it were a tree providing shelter—bow down before the son of the Lord of the Immortals.
Rāma: Noble lady, to the right of your hand is a very great mass of fire; what is this?
O ascetic, this daughter was bestowed by Prince Lakṣmaṇa upon that Yojanabāhu.
Rāma: Well done!
Lakṣmaṇa: Noble brother, look, look!
From being satiated, the broad spurts of blood boil; from the gory splashing, the long bones emit a pungent stench as skin and flesh fall away;
and then, from the dissolution of the fat, waves of bubbles surge upward.
How wondrous, how marvelous! This certain divine being arises from here, from his abode in the cremation ground.
(Entering, a man: Victory, victory to the divine Rāma!
I am Danu by name, the son of Śrī, who fell into the state of a Rākṣasa due to a curse;
having had my head severed by the weapon of Indra, I am purified by seeking refuge in you. 34.
Rāma: This is pleasing to us.

Danu: O Rāma, this forest had been made poisonous by me at the instigation of Mālyavān for the purpose of bringing you here. Enough of dwelling upon that past ignominy. But now, through your power, my innate light has awakened, and something remains obscure to me even as it appears before my eyes. This I shall relate to you, who have performed such great kindnesses, so that you may be enlightened. Having been entreated by Mālyavān, Vālī is being employed to slay you;
yet he, too, out of regard for his friendship with Rāvaṇa, hesitates. (35)
Rāma: This indeed is the path of those established in righteous conduct;
such a person does not maintain neutrality in a friend's cause.
My mind, too, seems filled with longing for this great hero. (36)
Others: "Where else but from Lord Rāma could these syllables have come?"
Rāma: My good man, you have shown great kindness. Now may this illustrious one rejoice for a long time in his own worlds.
(Daśaratha exits.
Lakṣmaṇa: Noble lady, what is the basis for the friendship between Vālin and Rāvaṇa?
O ascetic!

When Kailāsa had been weighed and the three worlds conquered, the son of Indra, having thrown the arrogant and attacking ten-faced Rāvaṇa—who was prepared for a wrestling match—into his armpit, completed his evening rites and then released him across the seven lords of rivers; and to that [Rāvaṇa], who had bowed down, submitted, and requested it, he granted friendship. (37)
Lakṣmaṇa: O evil-souled one, disgrace to the family of Paulastya! This is the extent of the excellence of your heroism, you who torment the Kṣatriyas.
Rāma: Thus is the world of living beings rendered wondrous by ever-increasing states of being.
Lakṣmaṇa: Noble lady, what is the name of this white mountain ahead?
O ascetic, this mountain is not a mass of glory belonging to the heroic Vālin;
it is the heap of bones of the buffalo-demon Dundubhi, the lord of the Daityas. (38)
Lakṣmaṇa: The paths have been blocked by him; therefore, let us go by avoiding him.
Rāma: Come now!
(He kicks with his foot.
Monk, it is marvelous!
That bull among monkeys, the delighter of Saṅkrandana, having crushed Dundubhi—the enemy of the gods—who was like a mountain of bones, cast him aside by the exertion of his pillar-like arms.
This [hand], which rivals a corpse that is suddenly turned pale by a dense cloud, now pierces through the Nirvindhya river from here, having struck it with a movement of the big toe.
Lakṣmaṇa: The forest, mountain, and terrain possess a tranquil, profound, dark-blue, and vast splendor.

O ascetic, these lands indeed extend as far as Ṛṣyamūka and Pampā; and likewise, ahead lies the hermitage of Mataṅga, where even now the venerable Vaiśvānara is kindled, though it be empty, with his equipment of special vessels for the Soma-cups present, and provided with strewn sacrificial grass, fuel, and the fragrance of clarified butter.
Rāma: The specific fruits of ascetic penances are of inconceivable success.
Ascetic: O King, look, look!

Here flow mountain streams with cool, clear water, fragrant from the blossoms shed by the cane thickets trodden upon by flocks of birds; their many currents are made resonant by stumbling against the groves of rose-apple trees darkened by the ripening weight of their fruit. (40)
Moreover:
Here, the deep, resonant growls of young bears dwelling in the caves produce a thickening of the air;
and the cold, pungent, and astringent scent of the oozing sap from the joints of sallakī trees, shattered and scattered by elephants, spreads through the atmosphere. //41//

Lakṣmaṇa: Why then does my noble brother stand here so suddenly, leaning upon his bow, his body held with such fortitude, his eyes overflowing with a mass of tears as he surveys the forests whose kadamba trees are being struck down by the violently blowing eastern winds?

Rāma: Child, do you not see? The Kadamba trees stand with their buds bursting open in full bloom; the peacocks perform their dance with unbroken throats; and a fresh rain-cloud, dark as the plumage of a mature Tāpiccha bird, now rests upon the peak of the mountain. (42)
Lakṣmaṇa:
(To himself) Might this noble brother not be diverted by some other sentiment?
(Offstage: Grandfather, turn back, turn back!
Even though the killing of a virtuous man would be improper by your command, it shall be carried out;
for you are indeed venerable as the teacher of my friend, and he who is the teacher of one’s teacher is a teacher himself. //43//
Lakṣmaṇa: Noble lady, who is this?
Ascetic: O King, look, look!
Bearing a beautiful garland made of golden lotuses given by Indra, he resembles a great rain-cloud charged with lightning and tinged by the twilight;
and as he moves swiftly through the sky, the son of Indra casts a splendor upon the mountain whose peak is struck by portents, like a streak of saffron upon the parting line of its brow. (44)
Lakṣmaṇa: Noble brother, noble brother! By good fortune, that dear friend Māghavata has arrived—he who delights in providing diversion for assemblies of heroes.
Rāma: (To himself) He is a great hero.
Then Vālin enters.
O Vālī!

Here indeed, I feel an intense despondency at the thought that my fate might shake this very pillar of Brahmā—a pillar whose basin is the Lokāloka mountain, from which the surging waters of the seven oceans overflow; a pillar from which the three worlds, with their joints nearly coming apart, would fall asunder along with the entire root of Pātāla uprooted; a pillar where the clusters of the sun and moon are cast down and the abundant flowers of the stars scatter. //45//

Thus, men who persist in what is improper are cast into the great abyss of calamity. Alas, what a grip! Having bound me since morning and dispatched me to Kiṣkindhā, this Mālyavān has now returned, reminding me of my friendship with the descendant of Pulastya and appointing me to the death of the venerable Raghudhvaja. Oh, the tragedy!

Alas, the misery! Out of wickedness, enemies who are masters of illusion have deceived the righteous guest—who is pure in his innate sincerity—just as he arrived at his own home, honored by the whole world, yet still regarded as their own.
In this matter, nothing appropriate was done, nor was even a single kind word spoken; fie on me, a sinner! How could I have made preparations for his execution as if he were an enemy? //46//

And just now my spies reported that Vibhīṣaṇa, without even informing Sugrīva, dispatched female mendicants to Rāma’s presence; and they returned with the news that the son of Daśaratha, having accepted the sovereignty of Laṅkā, is staying here in the vicinity of Mataṅga’s hermitage. Very well, I shall descend.

(He acts accordingly. Ho there! Who is present? I have come here to behold the one who has conquered Paraśurāma, who delights in truth and righteousness, the treasure-house of virtues, and the most beautiful one.
And there the eye becomes fruitful; when it is afflicted there, the scratching of an itch on the temple becomes delightful. //47//
Rāma: Dear Saumitri, inform the illustrious one that I am standing here.
Lakṣmaṇa:
(Approaching) Here stands my noble brother; let the illustrious one draw near.
Vālin: But is this indeed that Lakṣmaṇa?
Lakṣmaṇa: Indeed so.
(As they approach.
Vālin:
(To himself.)

This very Rāma, who is delightful through his conduct, the sole hero of righteousness, and the preeminent among men, surpasses all others—who are themselves incomparable—by means of his own most wonderful deeds. (48)
(Aloud: O Rāma, you have been seen by me for joy and wonder, or perhaps for sorrow; yet now, how can there be any thirst in my eyes for the sight of you?
I am no longer within the range of the happiness of your company; so why these vain words? Let the bow be drawn in this hand, which is renowned for subduing the son of Jamadagni.
Rāma: By good fortune you have been seen today; this is indeed appropriate. However, while you are unarmed, how can Rāma remain armed? (50)
Vālin: (Laughing) O great kṣatriya, why do you show such compassion toward us, who are not even worthy of pity?
We are already known throughout the worlds by our deeds; what need is there to speak with words? Be on your guard! It is true: you are indeed a human being.
We generally achieve victory without being obstructed by weapons; if you have a desire for them, remain at ease, for there are mountains where monkeys are armed with weapons.
Therefore, let us both ascend this high ground.
Lakṣmaṇa: Noble brother, it is as the illustrious one has said; the laws of war are established by the conventions of one's own class.
Vālin and Rāma:
(Addressing each other) Granted, a great festival of heroic discourse with you is indeed praiseworthy; yet—
But now that you have passed away, the earth is without a hero.
(Walking about, they both exit.
Lakṣmaṇa: How is it that the son of Indra has become enraged at the twanging of the bow? For thus he is:

his roar is as terrible as the thundering of a roaring rain-cloud, deep with its incessant onset; humming within, his mouth is wide open with a yawn like a cluster of *guñjā* berries, and the entire circle of the quarters of the world is clearly revealed.

With his tail—the banner of which is tawny like a spreading lightning flash, raised high and bristling with fury—he shakes his body, spreading it wide out of pride so as to cover the very lap of the sky. //53//
(Offstage: Vibhīṣaṇa, Vibhīṣaṇa!
This sound is surely that of the noble Vālin, as fierce as the thundering of fresh clouds;
and whence comes this terrifying twang of a bowstring? Has Hara discharged his Pināka bow? (54)
Lakṣmaṇa: Noble lady, who indeed is this?
Monks! Indeed, this Sugrīva, the friend of Vibhīṣaṇa, pursues the combat with both reflection and fury; and all the troop-leaders are descending from the mountain caves.
Lakṣmaṇa: In that case, I too must now string my bow.
O ascetic, this is the arrow that, having pierced through the sands, the drum, the hollow, the seventy palm trees, the mountain, and the surface of the earth, now lies within Rāma’s quiver.
(Offstage:
May the mind of Paulastya and Sugrīva be appeased through my oath and my betrayal. O heroic monkeys, may there be peace for you; I am indeed that very Lord.
This is my aspiration today: that I, who am the son of the Sun, may obtain the noble death of a hero at the hands of Rāma. He who is this one is your child, Aṅgada. //55//

Lakṣmaṇa: Therefore, here is the son of Śakra, even in this state, blazing with the glory of a hero; he is watched by the troop-leaders who, restrained by the unbearable pain arising from the violation of their warrior’s code of honor once freed from the constraints of their followers’ commands, hold back their tears out of partiality for their noble brother; his physical beauty is entreated by Vibhīṣaṇa, who is bound by an oath against betraying him; the force of the agony from the severing of his vital organs caused by the harsh blow—though suppressed by great effort—is made to appear as a golden lotus-garland upon his own neck, which serves as a collar encircled by Sugrīva’s neck under the pretext of an embrace; thus, even in this condition, he shines with the splendor of a hero.
(Then enter Sugrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, Vālin, and Rāma.)

Rāma: Alas! Having struck down even such men as these—possessing noble lineage, heroism, fame, and conduct; endowed with holy splendor; and being the immense treasures of the mountains that are their families—the cruel, all-devouring, and perverse Fate now grinds them down in its bitter fruition. (56)
Vālin: Child Vibhīṣaṇa! Look, look! The garland of a thousand lotuses shines most beautifully upon the chest of dear Sugrīva.
Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa:
(Aside) What is this cruel reversal of fate, as sudden and harsh as a bolt of lightning from a clear sky?
How can the Noble One be transgressed by us, who have been bound by oaths? How must we conduct ourselves? //57//
Vālin: Rāmabhadra, Rāmabhadra!
Rāma: Noble sir, here I am.
O Vālin, since by fate I have formed a friendship with this person— even one not intended as a friend— I am now, as if freed from my debt to my life-breaths,
ready to do whatever else is appropriate for the virtuous and for you, O mass of excellence, even at the cost of my life, according to my power. (58)
(Rāma stands with modesty, shame, and sorrow.
(Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa [aside]: Noble ascetic, how is it that this result for us from the divine Rāma is like emerging from a pool of nectar?
O ascetic, it is said that Mālyavān spoke thus.
(Thus he whispers into both ears. Vālin: Dear Sugrīva!
(Sugrīva acts out the choking of his tears.
Vālī: Sugrīva, is it not so? Ah, you have become an adversary!
Sugrīva: (With compassion) Noble sir, noble sir, be gracious; give me your command.
Vālī: Child, tell me, who am I to you?
Sugrīva is both my teacher and my master.
Vālin: But who are you to me?
Sugrīva is a child and a servant.
Vālin: Child, tell me, what is our mutual duty toward one another?
Sugrīva said: "May you have mastery over me, and may I be under your control."
Vālī: (Taking him by the hand) In that case, you are given to Rāma. O Rāma, surely he should be accepted!
Rāma and Sugrīva: For who indeed would not hold in high esteem the word of a venerable teacher?
Vibhīṣaṇa: Oh, what a concise summary, perfectly pure in its logical consistency with the Dharma, even though it covers such an extensive subject!
Vālin: Child Sugrīva, now, according to the words of the *Dharmapārāyaṇa* studied from your preceptor Jāmbavat, the son of Brahmā, what kind of dharma of friendship have you learned?

Sugrīva said: "To act for the benefit of others even at the cost of one's own life, to be free from malice, to avoid deceit, and to bestow what is pleasing upon them as if it were for oneself—this is the great vow of friendship. (59)
Vālin: O Rāmabhadra, this very same tradition belongs to you as well, descending from the venerable Vasiṣṭha, the family priest of the lineage of the thousand-rayed sun.
Rāma: Noble sir, indeed so it is.

Vālī: Therefore, by this law of friendship, you two must conduct yourselves toward one another. Out of regard for me, let a formal bond be established; for an agreement witnessed by fire cannot be transgressed, and here is the very fire of Mataṅga’s sacrifice at hand.
Rāma and Sugrīva:
(Taking each other's hands) Our friendship has been consummated at the sacred sacrificial fire of Mataṅga.
May your heart be mine alone, and may my heart be yours alone.
Vālin: O Rāmabhadra, this dear Vibhīṣaṇa was indeed promised the sovereignty of Laṅkā by you in the presence of the female ascetic.
Vibhīṣaṇa:
(With shame and apprehension) How have I been discovered?
O Śramaṇa and Lakṣmaṇa! Oh, what keenness of vision in your spies!
Rāma: Indeed so.
Vibhīṣaṇa: In that case, may the Lord be gracious.
(Thus he bows.
Sugrīva: Even by me the account of the ascetic was unknown; that it has now borne fruit, I consider my purpose achieved.
Rāma: O dear friends, the great kings Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa, here now is the son of Sumitrā for you both.
Lakṣmaṇa: Here is Lakṣmaṇa; he salutes you.
Both: Come, come, my child!
(Thus, having embraced her.
Śramaṇā: Your acceptance is exceedingly profound and full of flavor.

Vālin: Child Vibhīṣaṇa, enough now with this self-interested reticence. This matter will inevitably turn out exactly so. For it has already been explained by my own story that Rāvaṇa simply does not exist. Even though the affection for one's offspring is equal, it is especially the duty of those who depend on their kin to attend to the welfare of Rāvaṇa. It was appropriate for the maternal grandfather to speak himself of Vibhīṣaṇa’s union with his beloved. For only great men truly understand the unseemly agitation of such as he, whose character is unfathomable.
Indeed, my vital breaths are faltering; therefore, may you lead me to the precipice at the end of life.
O Nīla and the others!
Alas, O Hero! Alas, O son of Maghavan! O you whose essence was as unshakable as Mount Mandara! O hero who had no rival in the world!
O you whose circle of mighty arms was fierce and skilled in crushing the arrogant Dundubhi and Niśumbha! You have gone—alas, alas! We are destroyed. (61)
(Thus, being restrained by them as they wept, he walks about.
Vālin: O noble ones, foremost among monkeys!
That sovereignty over Sugrīva and Aṅgada which exists here is indeed your own benevolence; yet, out of affection for me alone, you must not disregard these two, for it is worthy of your greatness.

Now that the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa has arrived, this salutation with joined palms is offered as a manifestation of affection; yet, may all be peaceful, for who are we in comparison to your heroic powers?
Moreover:

those crushings of pairs of world-elephants whose ears are turned toward the quarters, those plunges into the netherworld through the openings of the ocean rent asunder by the lashing of their tails, and that which is so well-suited to the monkey-like prowess, the manly valor, the affection, and the majesty of you who have uprooted your enemies with your arms—do not let that be forgotten by you! 63.
(Thus they all exit.
